Forscutt’s Sketch: its last leaf, and page citations. A check of the manuscript on microfilm adds to the Repositories entry: the Historian’s Office bought the “Sketch of Joseph Morris” from Forscutt in June 1902, the manuscript breaks off at p. 54, and on its last leaf Forscutt writes that he burned a longer history of forty-six chapters. Corrections: page citations to the Sketch now follow Forscutt’s own numbering: the passage on an attack “Mountain Meadow fashion” is on p. 40 (not pp. 40–41); his dating of the first revelation is on pp. 7–11 (not 8–12); and the court-martial passages are on pp. 28–29 and 34–35.

Forscutt’s diary at the fort, and the date of his Sketch. Mark H. Forscutt’s journals (Mark Hill Forscutt Collection, Vault MSS 811, L. Tom Perry Special Collections, Harold B. Lee Library, Brigham Young University) have been read for their Morrisite content. His pocket diary kept at Kington Fort adds to the Chronology for December 1861 to April 1862: Lot Smith’s demand for the court-martial fines, the revelations of mid-December, the posse that could not be raised, the consecration vote of December 29, the Richards abduction, Merrill’s “Starve ’em out,” and the whipping of Christian Lundgreen. His later journals date the “Sketch of Joseph Morris” to 1884–85, written for Kate Field’s book on Mormonism (see Repositories). New roll notes for Lundgreen, Peter Moss, Niels Jacobson, William Richards, William Harris and James Mather; Almerin Grow’s converts at St. Louis in 1867; and a new research question, What does Forscutt’s shorthand diary say about the spring of 1862?, which credits Alan Bernthal-Hooker for working out Forscutt’s shorthand.

Morris on the resurrection and the worlds; the two Montana stakes. Two Morris pieces copied into Swedish by Emanuel Strom in 1872 are now on the Teachings page: an explanation of the diagram given at Weber in 1861, which puts Joseph Smith in the Terrestrial world presiding over the spirits of the dead, and an article teaching that the resurrection “takes place by birth” to immortal parents, close to the “baby resurrection” Brigham Young rejected (see also Where did the Morrisite teaching of reincarnation come from?). The movement at a glance notes now describe the two Montana stakes and their agreement of May 10, 1877, and add two mentions of Nels Damander. The Omaha & Council Bluffs entry under Places notes the Reorganized and Adventist missions among the Danes who stayed, and S. P. Guhl’s letter of November 1871 is now cited as Andrew Hendrikson’s copy of March 1872. Translations from the Swedish and Danish are generated by Claude.

The Morrisites and Mountain Meadows. Morris’s catechism “Keys of the Priesthood” names George A. Smith as Cain’s heir and a Judas among the apostles, and Forscutt says Morris made Smith “the moving spirit” of the Mountain Meadows Massacre (Teachings). The Morrisite War page adds the camp’s fear in 1861 of an attack “Mountain Meadow fashion,” and, from Burton’s trial of 1879, a Morrisite’s testimony that Mrs. Swanee cried out “is this going to be another Mountain Meadows Massacre” before she was shot, the prosecutor’s argument that the camp expected to be killed, and the prosecution’s link to the federal case against John D. Lee. The two 1879 reports are added to Newspapers and John Codman’s The Mormon Country (1874) to the Bibliography.

Where the dead of Kington Fort were buried. The Salt Lake City Cemetery interment register lists John Banks (no. 1470) next to Joseph Morris in the strangers’ ground, but none of the Morrisite women killed at the fort, by the first cannon shot or at the surrender; they were presumably buried elsewhere, perhaps at the fort or in South Weber. See Who died at Kington Fort?

A split in the Montana church. The movement at a glance chart now shows the group that followed William M. James after the April 1886 assembly elected George Thompson president. James, who claimed the presidency for life on the strength of Williams’s envelope “I leave you in charge,” was suspended for “usurpation of authority”; with the officers of Stake No. 1 he kept meeting at Warm Springs, told the court in May 1890 that he and his followers were “as much a part of the church,” and would rejoin only on his own terms (Church History Library, MS 32226 and MS 31876). The chart’s description also notes S. P. Guhl’s break with Williams in 1871, and, in a new paragraph under the chart, the breaks and rival claimants that left no lasting body, among them Nels Damander, who turned against Williams in 1873, and Joseph Warner, who in 1875 prophesied a gathering to Weber (see Who was “Brother Warner”?).

The Morrisite War, on its own page. A new page gathers what the guide has on the siege of Kington Fort, June 13–15, 1862: why the posse came, the three days, the dead, the prisoners and the 1863 trials, and Burton’s trial of 1879, with sources. The Glossary adds Consecration, the Oath of 1862 and the Adam–God teaching, and the site search now suggests the likely name when a search is misspelled (“Chrisoffersen” finds Christoffersen). See The Morrisite War.

Where they went: Omaha, Council Bluffs and Montana. The map now places members of the roll at Omaha and Council Bluffs in 1869 from the two congregations’ Danish registers (Church History Library, MS 32226), among them Rasmus Rasmussen, Christian Lundgreen, Anders and Karen Maria Sørensen, S. P. Guhl and Hans Knudsen; four in the Montana church’s membership record begun in 1874; Josiah D. Price in Oneida County, Idaho, in 1867; and John R. Eardley at Salinas, California, in 1878. Most of the register matches rest on name, birthplace and a South Weber baptism, and are shown as probable. Stops in England (William P. Thomas, 1869; Eardley, 1873) are pinned at the map’s right edge. Three uncertain matches, Elisa Christensen, “Maria Fellows, formerly Maria Guhl,” and a “Mary Larsen” in Montana, are drawn with dashed outlines so that anyone who can settle them will see them; please write if you can. See Where they went.

Josiah D. Price, the “431st person.” Price’s journal (Community of Christ Library Archives, P26-22 f1) records his baptism on December 3, 1861, by William Davies and Edward Lloyd, as the 431st person in the church, more than the 430 names on the printed roll; the consecration of property on December 30, 1861; and the oath sworn twelve at a time on February 12, 1862. He also put Morris’s ordinances and oath into Welsh. See the Chronology, Teachings and the roll. Also new: Brigham Young’s rejection of the “baby resurrection” in the At a glance table, and Kenneth Godfrey’s papers, with his article on Robert T. Burton’s trial, in Repositories.

Teachings at a glance. The Teachings page now opens with a table setting what Joseph Smith, Brigham Young, Joseph Morris, George Williams and Joseph Smith III taught or did on nine topics, from succession and the gathering place to plural marriage, women and the spiritual gifts. The Morrisite entries link to their sources on the page; on phones the table shows as cards.

What Williams kept and changed. Teachings now opens George Williams’s section with a comparison to Morris: what he kept (the order of sevens, birthrights, the diagram, the robe), and what he changed (the gathering moved from “the land of promise” to Montana, temple ordinances brought into the present, no more dates for Christ’s coming, salvation for nearly all, tongues restricted). The note on the Adam–God teaching now traces part of it to Morris’s own catechism on Genesis.

Coordinates on the site maps. On each place page’s site map, pointing at a marker or a land tract now shows its name, dates and coordinates (for tracts, the legal description too), and a readout under the map gives the latitude and longitude under the cursor.

Clearer site maps. On the Places map, the site-map previews and the maps on each place page no longer let place names overlap: each label now moves to the nearest clear spot beside its marker, and in the small previews minor labels give way to the places themselves.

Williams and Morris on plural marriage. Teachings and the marriage question now note that George Williams departed from Morris’s rule of one wife for eternity: he kept the household he had formed as a Latter-day Saint and in 1871 taught plurality in the eternities.

A clearer animated map. On the Where they went map, place names no longer crowd or overlap: long names are shortened, places a few miles apart share one label (the Kington Fort area now takes in South Weber and Slaterville, and Austin the rest of Lander County), and each label is set clear of the dots, the state names and the other labels. A list under the map gives every place shown in the chosen year.

The siege revelation, the 1863 prophecy, and two corrections. The Chronology adds Morris’s revelation of June 15, 1862, promising deliverance that day, and a prophecy in tongues given at Great Salt Lake City during the trials of March 1863, both from the Joseph Morris Papers (Community of Christ Library Archives, P11-1 f5). Teachings notes the manuscript copies of Morris’s rod inscription and the formula shared by the numbered rods and the bishop’s robe. Corrections to yesterday’s Repositories entry: the letter on the tides was written from Camp Douglas in 1869 (San Leandro was the dateline of the newspaper it answered), and the sceptre inscription is the text already known from Morris’s rod, not a new one.

Morris’s undated instructions. A folder of copies among the Joseph Morris Papers (Community of Christ Library Archives, P11-1 f6) was checked against The Spirit Prevails. From it: the marriage covenant “for time” of August 1861, set beside the prophet’s sealing “for time and all eternity” (Questions); the prophecy of December 21, 1860, of no endowment “in this place” and a law to govern the nations (Chronology); and an inscription for the prophet’s sceptre that is not in the book (Repositories).

The move into the RLDS Church. The question on why some Morrisites joined the Reorganized Church is rewritten as How and why did Morrisites join the RLDS Church? It now traces the move in four stages, from Utah and Idaho soon after the siege to the last generation at Race Track around 1919–20, drawing on new items from the Community of Christ Library Archives: Charles W. Wandell’s letters of 1873 on the “about twelve Morrisites” at San Juan, California, and their St. Ann’s Hill records; Joseph Warner’s letter of 1877 to the Saints’ Herald; and the RLDS Deer Lodge Branch register, which shows three former Omaha Morrisites baptized in 1887–90. The chronology adds 1873 and 1881–90, the lineage chart now runs to the 1920s, and Repositories lists the new items. The People page adds the three Omaha Morrisites, Peter Nielsen, Niels Jensen and Niels Thorkelsen.

Correction: “The Lord’s Supper.” The Teachings page quoted Williams’s 1881 ruling on the sacrament as “none partake of it but the Church in fair standing.” Both manuscripts read “outside the Church in fair standing”; the quotation is corrected. The page now dates the ruling to his answer to the council’s meeting of November 10, 1881, and adds his teaching in the same answer that the bread and wine were Christ’s “real body and blood,” by a principle “beyond the conception of men in mortality,” to be taken “even every week if it could be.” Repositories notes the copy made by John R. Eardley.

The last of the Montana minutes. The remaining pages of the 1881 council minutes show that Sister Rasmussen, ordained High Priestess in 1877, had died by March 1881 with no successor appointed (Questions), and that Emanuel Strom refused the sacrament from Erik Eliason that spring (People). Translations from the Danish are generated by Claude.

The Race Track council, 1876 and 1880. The rest of the council minutes for 1876 and 1880 add to the chronology the first recorded keeping of the 14th of February in Montana (1880), the council’s decision to hold Danish and English meetings in turn, and the arrival of Williams’s daughter Adelaide in Montana in 1880 (also in the Prophet Cainan entry); and, on the People page, more on Emanuel Strom and Johan Helström, who both sat on the council. Translations from the Danish are generated by Claude.

The Danish and Swedish copies; a correction. Correction: the chronology dated Williams’s instructions for organizing in Montana to the spring of 1872. Hendrikson’s Danish copy shows they were written on August 2, 1871; the surviving English pages, filed with the 1872 letters, are the second half of the same letter. The entry now stands under 1871 and adds Williams’s answer on “the object of gathering together in Montana.” Also new: on the Teachings page, Williams’s charge of November 1871 that Brigham Young had “a fearful reckoning to answer for causing to be slain” Morris; in the chronology, a letter of 1875 to the Omaha Morrisites from Barnet Moses Giles, another claimant; on the People page, Emanuel Strom (1846–1929) and his father-in-law Johan Helström, very probably the Johan Helström baptized at Fremont in 1871; Williams’s August 1871 counsel in the roll note for John Merrick; and fuller descriptions of Strom’s and Niels Jensen’s record books in Repositories.

Williams’s letter to “Bro. Robert” dated. The letter the Teachings page quoted as written to “Bro. Robert” about 1871 is headed “Loughboro, Feby 7th 1871, My dear Bro. Robert (Ford)” and called the “First Epistle of Cainan to Robert Ford”; the citations are corrected, and Repositories notes the likely link to the Robert Henry Ford of MS 5576. The Teachings page also adds Williams’s letter of April 1866 on an account for the sisters of “their position in the Priesthood … their equal privileges … their voice in their own assemblies,” held back for the time.

Williams’s letters to Montana, 1878–81, finished. The chronology for January 1879 adds Williams’s hope of still coming to Montana and his word that the Lord’s House was “not the only House of Prayer for Montana”; the Teachings page adds George Thompson’s report of a saying of Morris, “Stick no stake but what you can easily pull up again,” and the Jordan as the setting of the Mahomet interview in Williams’s 1877 retelling.

“Writings of Cainan, circa 1867–1872.” This folder dates Williams’s “Interview with Mahomet” to his journal of 1867 and places it at the mouth of Little Cottonwood Canyon, and holds the English original of the first chapter of the St. Ann’s Hill records, a Deer Lodge copy of March 1872, and the third chapter, “Chambers of the Dead” (see Teachings and Repositories).

Williams’s letters to Montana, 1876–77, finished. The Teachings page adds his reading of Brigham Young’s death in 1877 (“some for John, some for Orson, some for Wilford”), his rule that new members be baptized “to the lesser priesthood” and their genealogy sent to him, and his account of early opponents as “almost Apostles.” The chronology for 1877 adds music and “little schools,” and the Nez Perce scare at Deer Lodge; the roll note for S. P. Guhl, Williams’s charge that Guhl and Poulsen sought St. Ann’s Hill chapters to “gain favor with young Joe.”

Williams’s letters of 1872–73 to Andrew Hendrikson. The last folder of his letters to Hendrikson places Williams at Stockport, Cheshire, in the spring of 1873, with John R. Eardley’s family (Prophet Cainan and the roll note for Eardley). The Teachings page adds his search in 1872 for a successor (“the longing for my mantle is amusing”) and his list of those “visited by these immortals”; the chronology, his instructions of spring 1872 for organizing in Montana; and the roll note for John Merrick, Merrick’s earlier visit to him at Cottonwood.

Williams’s letters of 1871 to Andrew Hendrikson. The Teachings page adds his teaching of February 1871 that a high priest becomes a God by “taking one Daughter of each God” over 144,000 missions, beside his statement of the same years that he “never taught the doctrine or counselled the practice” of polygamy; his Paradise of partial faiths (“the Pope … Luther … Swedenborg … Brigham … young Joseph”); the high priests “not after the order of Seth nor Melchisedec” who bring the sciences; and the first chapter of the St. Ann’s Hill records, sent to Montana in July 1871, the earliest date found for them. The chronology adds Williams reading the Salt Lake Tribune, and the RLDS question under Questions his approval of the Omaha council’s action on Marie Mortensen. Correction: the earlier item today called Mortensen’s 1870 title seven years earlier than any High Priestess the guide had found; Theodora signed herself “High Priestess in England” in 1874, so it is four years earlier. The item is corrected.

Williams’s letters of 1870 to Andrew Hendrikson. Williams called Marie Mortensen the Omaha congregation’s “High Priestess” in 1870, four years before Theodora, the “High Priestess in England” of 1874 (corrected the same day; the item first said seven years) (see Teachings, the Omaha entry under Places, and the RLDS question under Questions). The Teachings page adds his account of Morris as the one who “gave the Diagram & revealed the two Priesthoods,” and the living raising or lowering their dead; the chronology adds “Abel’s Priesthood,” the English meetings of 1870, Almerin Grow’s own letter on his mission to Turkey, and Williams on the Godbeites; the Prophet Cainan entry adds the grasshopper year of 1870.

Williams’s letters of 1869 to Andrew Hendrikson and the Omaha church. A Danish record of January 26, 1869, is now the earliest witness that Enos meant Joseph Smith, and Williams’s own letters of that autumn speak of “Joseph the first, Joseph the second and the Lord’s Servant” (see Teachings, where the great and the common salvation is now dated from June 1869). The chronology adds Williams near Betchworth Castle, Surrey, in the autumn of 1869 and, apparently, in Wales by December. His family was in the 8th Ward by December 1869, not first in 1871 (Prophet Cainan). The roll notes for S. P. Guhl and the list entry for Andrew Hendrikson are expanded.

Williams’s letters to Montana, 1874–75. The rest of the folder adds to Teachings Williams’s teaching that “all will be saved except the fallen spirits or Sons of Perdition,” his doctrine of mortality as the purification of spirits “not valiant” in the first estate, his reply of September 1874 to his family’s accusations, and his call for a presiding sister in each stake; to the question on Brother Warner, Williams’s own warning of February 1875; and to the chronology, his plan of 1874 to come to Montana.

George Thompson’s letters and the Montana minutes, 1881–84. Thompson’s letters to William P. Thomas (1869–83) identify the “Gudmanson” of 1868 as Gudmund Gudmundson, give an 1869 witness that Seth and Enos meant Morris and Joseph Smith, and add his expectation of Morris’s return “about the year 1902” an endowment-like rite at Derby in 1869, and his memory that Morris “fell by the School house” (see Teachings). The Race Track minutes add the council’s removal of the dissenters on May 26, 1883, George Johnson’s appointment as bishop that day, the council’s vote of January 1882 upholding Thompson as Williams’s writer, and Cainan’s counsel against dance places (chronology). A roll note for George Thompson is new.

Williams’s marriages checked. The Rotherham parish register records Williams’s marriage to Susannah Woolfitt at Rotherham Minster on September 8, 1846, and the 1860 census lists him, Susannah and Louisa in one Salt Lake household; the 1857 marriage to Louisa King given in Family Tree is still without a record (see Teachings).

Williams’s household and Adelaide. FamilySearch Family Tree records two marriages for George Williams, to Susannah Woolfitt at Rotherham in 1846 and to Louisa King at Salt Lake City in 1857, and the 1880 census finds the two women in one Salt Lake household (see Teachings and Prophet Cainan). His daughter Adelaide never married the son of William James; she died at Los Angeles in 1947. Correction: the guide gave two forms of Adelaide’s name. The census and the California death index show she was Adelaide M[atilda] Williams; “Susanna Louisa Adelaide” named the household’s three women.

Williams’s last letters, 1880–82. His daughter Adelaide joined the Montana church and lived with the Daniel James family, and William James proposed a match with his son (see the chronology, 1882–83); Williams spent 1880–81 at Wrawby, Lincolnshire (Prophet Cainan); and George Thompson wrote in 1882 that baptisms at Weber needed no repeating (Teachings).

Brother Warner identified. A letter of John R. Eardley of November 1875 names the prophet of the 1876 gathering to Weber as “Bro. Warner—the German brother,” who claimed “the Presidency of the Apostleship” and to be “President of Germany.” He was almost certainly Joseph Warner of South Weber; the question under Questions is now marked answered, with only his manuscript still unaccounted for.

Williams’s letters of 1870–73. They add help sent by the Omaha and Montana Saints to his family in Salt Lake City, his requests for hymns from Margaret Thomas and John Bowen (see Teachings), and notes on Guhl, Bowen, Eardley and Moss in the roll.

A letter from Eardley, 1878. John R. Eardley’s letter to Williams from Hollister, California, in May 1878 adds to the roll notes for Joseph Moss (who froze to death near Austin, Nevada), R. J. Livingstone (Davies’s spokesman at Walla Walla, already doubting him), Svend Hegg, John Bowen and William W. Davies, whom Williams had ordained; and to the chronology, Almerin Grow’s turn to George Dove.

Williams in 1868. His letters of 1868 to Montana add to the chronology: money carried to him by W. P. Thomas, “the rebels Dow, Davies, Gudmanson” whom he had sent out as ministers, and a plot against his life that he gave as the reason he did not go to Montana. Correction: the guide quoted Williams in 1875 as writing that Parson, Livingstone and “Davy Dove” “attempted a Priesthood of their own”; the manuscript reads “Davy, Dove [or Dow]” and “attempted a business of their own.”

A poem on the siege, 1865. In a letter of November 1865 George Williams wrote an unfinished poem on the siege, “The Mormons came down like a wolf on the fold,” now quoted in the chronology. His letters of 1866–67 add a failed invitation to Montana in 1867, S. P. Guhl presiding at Virginia City, and an early mention of “the female Priesthood” (see Teachings).

The Anderson family. A portrait of Niels and Mary Christoffersen Anderson with their eight children is now under Images, beside the photograph of their house.

Joseph Warner, visionary. At Burton’s trial in 1879 Joseph Warner of South Weber testified that a vision of Joseph Smith had got him cut off from the Latter-day Saint church before he joined Morris in 1861, and read the court a sermon of his own; he died at South Weber in 1893, probably in September, “an indigent person” who left “no relatives” and a manuscript, according to the county court minutes. He was very probably the “Brother Warner” who prophesied in 1875 (see Questions). Mary Anderson’s testimony at the same trial adds a name to Who died at Kington Fort?

The Beck family. The entries for Lars P. Beck and his wife Maria, members of the Montana church from their baptism at Fremont, Nebraska, in 1871, now give their marriage, dates and children, and a new entry adds Lars’s brother Nels J. Beck, a trustee of the Lord’s House in 1887. With thanks to the Richardson family, who shared a family tree compiled by descendants.

The Andersons at Soda Springs. A photograph of Niels Anderson and Mary Christoffersen Anderson in front of a log house at Soda Springs, with a young woman believed to be their daughter, is now under Images.

Letters to Margaret and William P. Thomas, 1866–1882. Williams’s letters to the Thomases of Warm Springs (Church History Library, MS 31876) add to the chronology a revelation of 1866 in the Deer Lodge Valley, Eardley in England in 1874, Rasmus Rasmussen there in 1876, and Williams’s last letter of March 1882; to Teachings, the presidency of “Seth, Enos & Cainan,” celestial names, the robe, the St. Ann’s Hill chapter “Chambers of the Dead” and the Masons; and to the Prophet Cainan, the break with his family in Salt Lake City. A new open question asks who “Brother Warner” was, who prophesied in 1875 that the Saints would gather to Weber in 1876; a likely candidate is Joseph Warner of South Weber, whose marker is in the photographs and who was living there in 1880. Correction: the guide said Williams gave his daughter Adelaide’s full name as “Susanna Louisa Adelaide Williams.” In April 1871 he named her Adelaide Matilda, thirteen, and gave “Susanna Louisa Adelaide Williams” as the address; but about 1870 he had addressed her as “Miss Susanna Louisa Adelaide Williams,” writing out “all the Christian names.” The two letters do not agree, so the guide now gives both. (Updated the same day.)

The letters of “The Elder,” 1891. The Salt Lake Tribune’s Morrisite letters of 1891 turn out to be part of a series of ten, “Charity for the Mormons,” printed on Sundays from May 31 to August 2 and signed “The Elder”; John R. Eardley wrote that they were John Parson’s. All ten are now listed on the Newspapers page with free links to Utah Digital Newspapers. The three on the Morrisites add to the Chronology (the meeting of February 11, 1861; the opening of the siege; Howard Egan at Deep Creek in 1863) and to Who died at Kington Fort?, Was Lot Smith at the siege? and the Farmington court-martial question. Correction: the Chronology and Parson’s roll note said the letters began in June and announced that his work would be “established this year”; the series began on May 31, and those words come from a private letter of Parson’s to Eardley.

Data release 1.2. The data files are now release 1.2. It adds four people to the list of others named as Morrisites (Anders and Karen Søndermark, Hans Knudsen and Carleton Fellows), expands the entries for Joseph Morris, Andrew Hendrikson and the Bowmans, corrects George Williams’s entry, and records Josiah Price’s later affiliation with the Reorganized Church. It is archived at Zenodo with the earlier releases (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24154693).

Why William James went to Nevada. A copy of a revelation of August 20, 1872, among the letters to William P. and Margaret Thomas (Church History Library, MS 31876), shows that James’s mission of 1872 was to help John D. Bowen of Austin, Nevada, keep his property; Bowen’s own letter of 1874 says he lost it anyway. Added to the Chronology under September 22, 1872, with Andrew Hendrikson’s baptism in the Missouri River at Omaha in January 1869 under 1869, and a roll note for John Bowen.

The Council Bluffs register. The Council Bluffs congregation’s register of 1869–71 (Church History Library, MS 32226) shows S. P. Guhl baptized at South Weber on August 7, 1861, by Peter Klemgaard and Jens Mikkelsen and confirmed by Morris, Richard Cook and John Banks, and identifies further roll members baptized at South Weber: Niels and Maren Larsen, Mikkel Christensen and probably Elisa (Lese) Christensen, and a Maria Guhl, later Fellows. See the roll notes and Who they were (Hans Knudsen, Carleton Fellows). Corrections to the Omaha entries of earlier tonight, from the draft of that register: Rasmus Rasmusson’s birthplace reads “Akkerup,” not “Akkrup”; Christian Lundgreen’s baptism (June 30, 1861) and confirmation by Morris are now certain; the Søndermarks were baptized by Morris and Mikkelsen and are entered in the draft as Anders and Karen Maria Sørensen; and Hans Petersen’s exclusion is dated only to 1870.

The Omaha register. The Omaha congregation’s own register of members, 1869–1872 (Church History Library, MS 32226), lists forty-two members with their birthplaces and baptisms, five of them at South Weber in 1861. It adds roll notes for Christian Lundgreen, Hans Petersen and Kershon (Kjersten) Peterson and to the note for Rasmus Rasmusson, and two Morrisites not on the roll, Anders and Karen Søndermark, baptized at South Weber on July 31, 1861, to Who they were. The register is described on Repositories.

The Montana church organized, 1872. The Montana council’s first minutebook (Church History Library, MS 32226) records the meeting of September 22, 1872, at William P. Thomas’s house on Warm Spring Creek that organized the church there under Williams’s instructions, with William James as president and Margaret Thomas as “Lady elect to preside over the Female Order.” See the Chronology, the Teachings and the roll notes for W. P. Thomas and William James.

Williams on polygamy, Idaho and Abel. A letter of George Williams of about 1871 in the Church History Library’s MS 32226 adds to the Teachings: his statement that he “never taught the doctrine or counselled the practice” of polygamy, a gathering “in Idaho” that was not permitted, the washing of feet, counsel on eating and drinking, an earlier account of Grow’s mission, and Adam’s future government with Abel as “the next Jesus Christ.”

Morris’s apostles in California, 1874. A letter of S. P. Guhl from Council Bluffs, August 11, 1874 (Church History Library, MS 31876), reports that Morris’s apostles had organized in California under John Parson, with R. J. Livingston and Alexander Dow as counselors. It is added to What became of the California congregation? and to the roll notes for Parson, Livingstone, Dow and Guhl.

Letters of 1872–1878. Hendrickson’s letters for 1872–1878 (Church History Library, MS 31876) show James Bowman, whose wife Isabella was killed at the surrender, still a believer at Soda Springs in 1878 and receiving Williams’s epistles, and mentioning “Joseph Morris’ Father in Law” nearby; and John R. Eardley at Salinas City, California, in December 1878. See Who they were and the roll note for Eardley. Correction: the entry for George Williams on Who they were still said that he prophesied in 1879 that Deer Lodge County would be the site of the Second Coming; it now follows his letter, as the Chronology does.

Reports from inside the camp, 1861–62. Informers’ reports to Brigham Young in his office files (Church History Library, CR 1234 1) add to the Chronology for May–December 1861: Morris’s claim, on May 12, 1861, to be “the Seventh Angel”; the revelation of May 11 calling believers to gather at South Weber; and a diagram already in use that spring. An onlooker’s letter describes the procession of May 30, 1862, and acting governor Frank Fuller’s letters of June 14 and 16, 1862, are added to the days of the siege. The Teachings page adds the confirmation by three men, the Holy Ghost as a “redeemed being,” a form for ordaining an “elect lady,” and the inscriptions on the numbered rods of office, copied on June 19, 1862. See also Where did the rituals come from? and the Glossary.

The Danish mission. Letters to Andrew Hendrickson of 1869–1871 (Church History Library, MS 31876) show a congregation of Williams’s followers in Copenhagen in 1871 and S. P. Guhl’s letter of November 1871 breaking with Williams; see the Chronology and the roll note for Guhl. The Places page now ends with a short note on places beyond the American West: England, Denmark and Constantinople.

The siege, day by day. A posse member’s account of the siege and the lists of prisoners in the Church History Library (CR 100 397, CR 1234 1) let the Chronology give the siege a day at a time, June 13–17, 1862. New: 149 men were taken, of whom 100 were brought to Salt Lake City and 49 released at the fort, among them eight, Mark H. Forscutt and John R. Eardley with them, who had given themselves up during the fighting. The posse member, John G. Chambers, gives a third account of the rolling battery and writes that Banks was killed with Morris at the surrender; both are noted under Who died at Kington Fort? and on the Kington Fort page. The files are described on Repositories.

Williams on Mahomet, the eight estates and the August feast. The rest of the record of letters from Cainan, 1873–1879 (Church History Library, MS 31876), has been read. New on the Teachings page: Williams’s account (1877) of a message from Mahomet to the Sultan, carried by Almerin Grow; his teaching (1880) of eight estates and of Adam as the savior of an earlier planet; a Montana copy of two chapters of the records he said he translated, with the “Mighty Goddess”; and his confirmation (1880) of William James’s proposal that the anniversary of the Lord’s House be kept as a feast, also in the Glossary. Correction: the Repositories page called Emanuel Strom’s 1872 copies of Williams’s epistles Danish translations; they are in Swedish.

The Montana church in the 1880s. Hendrickson’s letters for 1880–1889 add to the Chronology: the dispute over the yearly election in 1884; the officers of Stake No. 1 who held out for William James in 1886; the Doves’ return to Montana in March 1887; John R. Eardley’s contacts with David Whitmer’s followers in 1887–89 and his journey to England in 1887; and George Thompson’s letters from Epping. See also How did Latter-day Saints, the Reorganized Church and the Morrisites live alongside one another? and the roll notes for Eardley and John Parson.

The Montana church, 1893–1901. From the last of the letters to Andrew Hendrickson: Eardley watching the Salt Lake Temple dedication against a prophecy he attributed to Morris, baptisms at Race Track on August 9, 1893, a shared meeting house in 1894, and the “threatened collapse” of 1901 (Chronology); and Hendrickson’s own view of the Son and the Father, 1897 (Teachings).

George Thompson’s sister. Jane Higham, on the roll with her husband Charles, was the elder sister of George Thompson, Williams’s companion in England and later president of the Montana church; Thompson settled near the Highams in Bingham County, Idaho, in 1891.

The Montana church in 1891. Eardley’s letters of 1891 add to the Chronology: John Parson’s weekly letters in the Salt Lake Tribune and his visit to the Deer Lodge Valley, the November court in the year “expected,” and the first open break at Warm Springs in December.

Morris’s diagram of the worlds. The Teachings page now shows “The Rounds of Eternity: Joseph Morris’ First Diagram,” from Eardley’s Gems of Inspiration (1899), and “Seth’s Diagram” from Williams’s record of letters of the 1870s, a hand-colored version with Swedish labels. A third version, a drawing in Josiah D. Price’s journal, is described there.

Records from the Community of Christ Library Archives. Josiah D. Price’s journal names the six men Morris baptized on April 6, 1861, and describes the drill and the four horsemen of May 1, 1862, the soldier’s oath of May 26 and the Foreshadowing procession of May 30. The Joseph Morris Papers, which appear to be Alexander Dow’s, add his account of the siege and his later life in St. Louis. See the Chronology, the Teachings page, Where did the rituals come from? and the Repositories.

The Doves and Davies. The movement at a glance chart now draws a line from William W. Davies to the Doves’ California congregation, as the chart’s description already said. James Dove’s A Few Items in the History of the Morrisites shows him joining Davies’s followers in San Francisco in 1868; the Chronology under 1873 now gives his account.

Correction: when the Doves organized. The movement at a glance chart said the Doves’ California congregation was a Church of the Firstborn “from 1873,” following Watson. James Dove’s own A Few Items in the History of the Morrisites places the organizing after April 7, 1874, and shows the church still active in 1892; the chart now reads “from c. 1874; active 1892,” and the Chronology gives both accounts. The chart’s description also now names the Emmonses, who joined the Reorganized Church in 1890.

Letters of 1890. Hendrickson’s letters for 1890 show a Montana family, the Emmonses, joining the Reorganized Church that year, and John R. Eardley conceding that Williams “was mistaken” in calling himself Daniel’s stone. See How did Latter-day Saints, the Reorganized Church and the Morrisites live alongside one another? and the Teachings.

W. P. Thomas and the Evans family. The roll note for W. P. Thomas now records that Find a Grave links him as the father of Evan Price Thomas (1845–1891), and that a 1945 account places him on Warm Springs Creek before Morgan Evans’s party arrived in 1865. The same account dates the Evans family’s arrival to August 1865 and their move to the site near Opportunity to the spring of 1866 (see the Bibliography entry for In the Shadow of Mount Haggin).

Letters of 1892. Hendrickson’s letters for 1892 include a printed copy of James Dove’s A Few Items in the History of the Morrisites, so it comes off the Wanted list. From it, the Chronology now has the Doves’ 1885 mission to Utah and Montana and their account of how The Spirit Prevails came to be printed. Refined date: John Parson’s death is now dated June 13, 1892, at the Larsens’ ranch near Deer Lodge (his page gave only the year and place). The Teachings add Thompson’s and Eardley’s hopes in 1892, and the Lord’s House glossary entry notes that it was still in use at the end of 1892.

The revelation of the two stakes, 1874. Williams’s epistle from Ashby of April 6, 1874 (Church History Library, MS 31876) contains the revelation that divided the Montana church into “two Stakes under one Head,” James and Hendrikson each to take charge of “those that are convenient unto him,” the source of the word disputed in 1876. The same letters show “the Sides of the North” in use by 1874 (the guide had said 1877), the first robe for William James and a “thanksgiving day” with singing and dancing. See the Chronology under the 1870s, the Teachings page and Where did the rituals come from?

Correction: who was Enos? The Teachings page said that Seth and Enos in Williams’s vision of 1862 were very probably Morris and John Banks. A letter of Williams’s of December 1881 says that Morris called Joseph Smith Enos, meaning that he “represented” him; Seth is Morris. The page is corrected.

Williams’s letters to Montana, 1878–1881. They give Thompson’s written appointment to act for Williams (July 14, 1881), sent to Montana for the Saints’ approval; the ladder of 144,000 names and Christ’s return of the kingdom to “the Father of the family, even Adam,” with a note on the Adam–God teaching; rites for blessing children and the sacrament; the Lord’s House as “a Temple in miniature”; and Beck’s visit to Williams at Cottonwood, which supports the phrenology fragment. See the Teachings page, the Chronology under 1880–81, the Glossary, and the questions on phrenology and on government by vote.

Correction: the charge against William P. Thomas. Earlier today the Chronology placed the charge against Thomas in 1877 and said no record of it had been found. The New North-West shows that a Deer Lodge grand jury indicted “Wm. P. Thomas” in December 1876 for assault with intent to do great bodily injury, and that a jury found him not guilty on December 21, 1876. The account is now under 1876 in the Chronology.

Williams’s letters to Montana, 1876–1878. His letters to William James and the Montana Saints (Church History Library, MS 31876) give the High Priestess ordained for Stake No. 2 in 1877; the white robe; the founding of the Court of the Lord’s House; the first request, in October 1877, for a building “to carry out Temple ordinances” and the words for its dedication in 1878; the October 1877 motion consigning Davies, Guhl and the Doves to “outer darkness”; the charge against William P. Thomas; his own words on the “keys of detection”; and his mockery of “come to Walla Walla and see my little Jesus.” See the Teachings page, the Chronology under 1876, 1877 and 1878–79, the Glossary, and the questions on women, on phrenology and on government by vote.

Correction: how the Church History Library folders are cited. The catalog does not number the folders of MS 31876, and this guide’s folder and item numbers counted them in two different ways, so some led to the wrong folder. Every MS 31876 citation now names the folder by its catalog title, for example “Minutes, 1876.”

The Montana church, 1882–1891, and Seth’s Diagram. The remaining Montana minutes (Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1882 to Minutes, 1891) have now been read, with the first letters of Williams to William James of 1876–77. New: the doctrine of birthrights set out by the church’s court in 1887; how the church met 1891, the year it had been taught to expect the Second Coming; prayer standing with hands raised; the 1887 election and the Lord’s House trustees; a proposal of 1891 to move the Lord’s House; Eardley as “first Counselor to Cainan in England”; and a description of “Seth’s Diagram.” See the Teachings page, the Chronology under 1876, 1886, 1887 and 1891, and the Glossary entries for the Lord’s House and the Prophet Cainan.

The Montana church in 1880–81. The Danish council minutes for 1880 and 1881 (Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1880 and Minutes, 1881) have been read in part. They give a robed William James administering the sacrament and looking for the coming of Christ in 1891, the first August 9 conference, word of the death of a son of Williams, Thompson writing Williams’s epistles by September 1881, Eardley preaching against brandy and tobacco, and a ruling of 1881 against speaking in tongues in public meetings. New in the Chronology under 1880–81, on the Teachings page under George Williams, and as first findings for What became of the spiritual gifts?

The Montana church in 1876. The Danish council minutes for 1876 (Church History Library, MS 31876, Minutes, 1876) have been read in part. They show William James away on a mission for Williams, the dispute over the two stakes when he returned in August, Williams’s call in November for proposals on a form of government, and the exclusion of a member who had lost faith in Cainan. New in the Chronology under 1876, with notes under Marriage on the Teachings page and on Dempsey Creek under Places.

George Morris on his brother Joseph. The reminiscences of Morris’s elder brother George (Church History Library, MS 1614) have now been read for this guide. They give Joseph’s life before Utah (England, St. Louis, Pittsburgh), his arrival in 1853, his early marriages, a private revelation offering George an apostleship, Brigham Young’s 1876 permission for proxy ordinances, and George’s verdict on Burton’s 1879 trial. See Documents and the Chronology.

The editor’s photographs are free to reuse. Photographs taken by the editor are now licensed under CC BY 4.0, like the guide’s text and data: credit “Eric Paul Rogers, Morrisite.org.” Photographs from other people and institutions still belong to their owners.

When the Montana church ended. Correction: the guide said, citing Anderson, that the Montana church disbanded in 1969 after a last annual gathering on August 6, 1969. Anderson dates the end to George Johnson’s death in 1954, when the Lord’s House was boarded up, and records a feast-day gathering of surviving Morrisites on August 9, 1969 (Revisited, pp. 212, 214, 218); the 1969 date for a formal disbanding comes from Utah State University’s finding aids. The guide also now credits the reading of the Deer Lodge prison as Ezekiel’s temple to Leland Jensen rather than to Neal Chase (pp. 216–18). See the Chronology and How and when did the Montana church end?

Watson’s Writings and Revelations among the essential works. Start here now lists Kirk Watson’s 2026 collection of writings by Morris, Williams, Davies and the Doves.

“Walla Walla Jesus.” The Glossary now explains the name, later given to William W. Davies’s son Arthur, whom Davies proclaimed the Messiah; a new question asks when the name was first used.

Teachings across the guide. Following the new Teachings page: the failed-prophecy, marriage and reincarnation questions have new first findings; the Chronology adds the consecration revelation of December 30, 1861, Davies’s “third dispensation” of 1866, George Dove’s Church of the Firstborn of 1873 and James Dove’s Treatise on Re-Incarnation of 1892; the Glossary adds “Sides of the North” and the order of seven angels; and the lineage chart now dates the Doves’ church from 1873.

A new page: what the Morrisites taught. Teachings summarizes the movement’s beliefs period by period, with sources: Joseph Morris on the coming of Christ, consecration, reincarnation, the spiritual gifts and marriage; George Williams, the Prophet Cainan, and “the Sides of the North”; the Montana church; William W. Davies’s Kingdom of Heaven; the Doves; and later echoes. It draws on The Spirit Prevails, Gems of Inspiration, Kirk Watson’s new edition, and Williams’s letters at the Church History Library.

Williams’s 1879 prophecy, from his own letter. Correction: the guide said that in January 1879 George Williams prophesied that Deer Lodge County would be the site of the Second Coming. His letter of January 6, 1879 (in a copy made by Andrew Hendrickson in 1883, Church History Library, MS 31876) names no county and no date: it calls the region where the Montana Saints lived “the Sides of the North,” where “the City of the great King” would come down before the Lord’s coming. The Chronology and the Glossary entry for the Prophet Cainan now say so.

Three new questions from the Deer Lodge Valley. The Questions page now asks where the Copper Village organ came from (a 2013 recording describes it as a Mason & Hamlin built about 1892, too late to have come from Utah or to date from the building of the Lord’s House), whether Gwendale was named for Gwenllian Evans, and whether the Evans and Thomas families of Gwendale were connected to the Morrisites.

Willow Glen Ranch in 2013. The Images page has seven photographs of the Willow Glen Ranch east of Anaconda, taken on July 8, 2013, and contributed by a reader. They show the barn, a cobblestone pillar, the stone cottage and the lane. This is the later stock farm of that name, not the Morrisite Willow Glen of the 1880s on Warm Springs Creek.

A new question: Morrisite teaching and Chad Daybell. The Questions page now asks whether there is a line from Morrisite teaching to Chad Daybell’s. It compares Williams’s 1869 assignments of earlier lives with Daybell’s past-life claims and notes the differences, above all Daybell’s “zombie” teaching, which has no counterpart in the Morrisite records. No evidence of descent is known.

Data release 1.1. The data files are now release 1.1. It corrects John Peter Lorensen’s entry, which had given a death in Nevada in 1870 that the records do not support, and adds George Johnson’s birth in Denmark in 1856. It is archived at Zenodo alongside release 1.0 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24139092).

Building the Lord’s House; Montana in 1873–74. Correction: the guide said the Lord’s House was begun in 1877. The council minutes (Church History Library, MS 31876) show the site was chosen only on February 24, 1878, when a joint council voted ten to five to build on Andrew Hendrikson’s land at Race Track. The House was built under Peder Jansen, used for Sunday meetings from the summer of 1879, and nearly paid for that October; the Chronology and the Glossary now say so. Also added to the Chronology: Stake No. 2’s founding meeting of July 12, 1874; the church in 1873, with William James on a mission in Nevada and the quarrel between William P. Thomas and Daniel James; a Fremont, Nebraska, branch, 1871–73 (now also shown in a small locator inset on the Omaha & Council Bluffs map, with Lincoln); and Sven Olson Hagg’s letter of March 1866, which shows Morrisites meeting in the Deer Lodge Valley that winter and William W. Davies already claiming spiritual gifts there. See also the roll notes for Hegg, Davies, Thomas, James and Eliason. The Danish passages are translated by Claude and not yet checked.

About the Danish translations. The translations of the Danish minutes, the 1869 record book and the Omaha minutebook quoted in this guide were generated by Claude, Anthropic’s AI model, from the Church History Library’s page images (MS 31876). No Danish reader has checked them yet, so treat them as provisional. Each citation now says so, and so does the collection’s entry under Repositories.

Omaha in 1871. The last pages of the Omaha minutebook show the congregation giving up Latter-day Saint-style conferences in March 1871, a leader of its sisters, Marie Mortensen, joining the Reorganized Church that May (the earliest such case yet found among Williams’s followers), and the book closing on June 4, 1871, as members prepared to move west. Its companion record book of 1869 records the earlier lives Williams assigned to the men he anointed. See Omaha & Council Bluffs under Places, the RLDS question under Questions, and Reincarnation in the Glossary.

The Omaha minutebook. The Danish minutebook of the Omaha and Council Bluffs church (Church History Library, MS 31876) tells how it was organized in February 1869, while George Williams passed through Omaha on his way to England, and names the Welsh missionary who went with William P. Thomas in 1869 as Daniel James, settling the question corrected earlier today. See Omaha & Council Bluffs under Places, the Chronology, and the roll notes for Rasmus Rasmusson, S. P. Guhl and W. P. Thomas.

The Lord’s House dedicated August 9, 1879. The Danish council minutes of the Race Track stake (Church History Library, MS 31876) date the dedication of the Lord’s House: in July 1882 the council planned to celebrate August 9 as the third anniversary of its dedication. They also show the council keeping February 14 as Williams’s birthday, and the Danish members’ debate before the 1883 vote. Added to the Chronology and the Glossary.

A correction: which James went to England. Earlier today the Chronology said that William James went with William P. Thomas to join Williams in England in 1869–70. George Thompson’s letter of July 29, 1869, addresses the two as “W. P. and D. J.,” so the Brother James was probably Daniel James, not William M. James; the entry is corrected. Thompson’s letters to Thomas (Church History Library, MS 31876) also place Thompson with Williams at Ashwicken in 1869 and give Williams’s age and the cause of his death, now in the Chronology and the Glossary.

Williams’s letters to Andrew Hendrikson. Williams’s letters of 1869–73 to Hendrikson and the Omaha church (Church History Library, MS 31876) show that William P. Thomas and a Brother James went to England to be with him and returned to Montana in 1870, give Williams’s own account of Almerin Grow’s mission to Constantinople and Jerusalem, and trace the move from Omaha to Montana in 1871–72. Added to the Chronology and to the roll notes for Rasmus Rasmusson, John Merrick and S. P. Guhl; John Merrick’s identification is raised from “Check” to “Probable.”

Williams in England, 1869–73. Williams’s letters of 1870–73 in the Church History Library (MS 31876) show that he left America about January 1869, leaving his family in Salt Lake City, and that his “Ashby” was Ashby by Brigg, Lincolnshire; they also name his daughter Adelaide. In 1873 he called “Burton and Lot Smith” “the murderers at Weber”; whether Lot Smith was at the siege is a new open question under Questions.

A correction: Montana by 1868. The Glossary said the Montana church regathered in the Deer Lodge Valley in the 1870s. A letter of George Williams dated December 14, 1868, is addressed to “Bro. James & Saints of the Most High in Montana,” so William James’s group was there, under that name, by 1868 (Church History Library, MS 31876). The Glossary is corrected and the Chronology has a new 1868 entry, which also notes that Williams was living in George Thompson’s house at Walthamstow by 1876. The roll note for Charles Higham adds his visit to Thompson in England about 1877.

Thompson at Williams’s side. In March 1882, as George Williams lay dying at Walthamstow, George Thompson answered the Montana church’s questions for him, explaining that Williams “was not really Cainan the son of Enos” but represented him, and promising to confirm the church’s choice of officers (Church History Library, MS 31876). Added to the Chronology, the Glossary and the Questions.

Thompson in England. George Thompson, elected president of the church in Montana in April 1886, was writing to the members that December from Thornwood Common, Epping, Essex, open to Joseph Smith III being “called through our Joseph” but not yet calling him a prophet. The letter is in the Church History Library’s Cainan letters (MS 31876) and is now in the Chronology and the Questions. The same letters show John R. Eardley planning, in February 1880, to open a store in Montana (see the roll note).

Williams’s last instructions. The Church History Library’s Cainan letters (MS 31876) hold George Williams’s own note of January 29, 1882, directing that William James be put before the church a year after his death, and an envelope to James inscribed “I leave you in charge after my decease,” the words James later relied on in claiming the presidency for life. Both are now in the Chronology. The same letters add to the roll notes for S. P. Guhl, who disputed James’s authority from Omaha in 1874, and for John Parson, William White and John Merrick, whom John R. Eardley reported on from California in 1875.

A correction: the Montana elections. This guide said, following Anderson, that William James was sustained as president in Montana in May 1882 and that George Thompson was elected president of the church on May 10, 1886. The Montana minutebook at the Church History Library records both elections at the yearly general assembly on April 25, the anniversary of George Williams’s death: James in 1883, by 19 votes to 10, and Thompson in 1886. The May dates are those of council meetings. The Chronology and Questions are corrected.

The Montana church’s own records. The Church History Library’s Church of the Firstborn records, now on the Repositories page and readable online, include the membership record kept from 1874 and the council minutes for 1881–1890. They give the date of Williams’s death in England (April 25, 1882), the two stakes on Warm Spring Creek and at Race Track, the meeting house at Willow Glen, the schisms of 1883 and 1886, the council’s notice in the New North-West of November 13, 1885, disowning the Doves of the California congregation (now on the Newspapers page), and an invitation in 1886 to use the Reorganized Church’s new meeting house in Deer Lodge City, which settles who built the church a newspaper had called Morrisite, now a first finding on one of the open questions. The membership record also strengthens the notes on several names on the roll: Ole Olsen, W. P. Thomas and Erick Eliason, and new notes for William James, Christian Anderson and Rasmus Rasmusson.

A correction: the Zbaraschuk paper. Tony Zbaraschuk’s 1989 paper on William W. Davies was written at Walla Walla College, not Whitman College as this guide said. Its acknowledgments thank his thesis advisor at Walla Walla College, and the Church History Library catalogs it the same way. The Bibliography is corrected.

Citations for your reference manager. The Bibliography and the Newspapers list can now be downloaded for Zotero, EndNote or Mendeley, as RIS, BibTeX or CSL-JSON: 109 books, articles, theses and media items, and 66 newspaper articles and reprints, each reprint noting the paper it was copied from. Each record keeps the citation exactly as it appears here.

A correction: Johan Peter Lorentzen. Earlier versions of this guide gave his death as 1870 in Nevada. Family Tree says only that he died before 1870, probably in Nevada; the date was an estimate misread as a year. His death date is now left blank on the roll, the people and Movements pages and in the data files, and a new roll note explains the evidence, including the 1870 census, which finds his children Charles and Josephine at Treasure City with no father in the household. The same misreading had crept into the new roll note on Ole Olsen’s wife Anne, which gave Family Tree’s date for her death as 1870; the tree, too, says only “before 1870,” with no source, so the 1902 account of her death in Wyoming in 1862 stands uncontradicted. That note is corrected.

George Johnson in 1902. A county biography of about 1902, Progressive Men of the State of Montana, says of George Johnson, later the last leader of the Montana church, that “Johnson and his family are members of the Morrisite church.” It also confirms that his wife, Josephine V. Oleson, was a daughter of Ole Olsen of the 1861–62 roll. Both entries are updated: Johnson under others named, and Ole Olsen on the roll.

Free to reuse, with credit. The guide’s own text and data are now licensed under CC BY 4.0, and the data files carry a release number and a list of changes, so a figure can be traced to the version it came from. Release 1.0 is archived at Zenodo with a permanent identifier, doi:10.5281/zenodo.24100263. Every name on the roll now has its own link (hover over a name and click #), pages can be saved to Zotero with one click, and pages print without menus and buttons. The About page now explains how corrections are made and what the guide does for accessibility.

item.title: 9 Nov 2026: The guide’s data, to download; Birthright by phrenology?; The Racetrack church in 2020; and 1 more

• The guide’s data, to download
  • Birthright by phrenology?
  • The Racetrack church in 2020
  • The missing pages of the Davies case

The guide’s data, to download. A new Data page offers the lists behind the roll, the person pages and the Where they went map as CSV files: the 1861–62 roll with FamilySearch matches, birthplaces, emigrating companies and later affiliations; documented whereabouts after 1862; family ties on the roll; and others named as Morrisites. Each comes with a description of its columns and their limits, and all four can be downloaded together. The page also shows how much is known so far about the people on the roll, where they were decade by decade, a table of the roll that can be sorted, filtered, shared by link and downloaded, and a tool for counting the roll by any two characteristics, with the unknowns shown.

Birthright by phrenology? A typescript fragment in the Morrisite collection at USU, printed in Kirk Watson’s edition of Morrisite writings (pp. 90–91), says that a prophet in hiding at Cottonwood read men’s priesthood by feeling their heads, and that no descendant of Cain would enter the Church. Watson, who brought it to the guide’s attention, identifies the prophet as the Prophet Cainan. The page also names a Niel Beck. See the new question of interpretation.

The Racetrack church in 2020. Ten photographs taken inside and outside the Lord’s House on August 16, 2020, contributed by a reader, extend the condition record between 2018 and the videos of 2026. They show the pulpit, benches and table still in place, and the hymnals and a 1931 Reorganized Church lesson quarterly left in the building. See Images. The Bibliography adds In the Shadow of Mount Haggin (1975), on the Evans family at Gwendale, and an Anaconda Standard article of 1935 that Patrick F. Morris cites.

The missing pages of the Davies case. Pages 133–157 of the 1880 case against Davies are not in the file at the Washington State Archives: archivist Lee Pierce confirms the whole file was scanned and that those pages were missing before it reached the archives. They may have left the courthouse with pages 158–195, which Whitman College later found and returned. See Repositories.

item.title: 8 Nov 2026: Corrections
item.description:
• Corrections

Corrections. A check of the guide against its sources led to several fixes. The chronology no longer gives a single death toll for the siege, and now says that John Banks died in custody on the evening of the surrender. The Glossary explains that “Church of the Firstborn” was not the name of Morris’s church in 1861: his revelations call it “my Church,” and Anderson gives the Church of Jesus Christ of Saints of the Most High. The roll no longer lists Joseph Morris’s wives as Mary and Karen: his wife Mary Olsen is probably the roll’s Mary Morris, and Karen Morris is not identified. Notes on Anne Bar now record that the sources disagree on whether her baby died. Citations of The Spirit Prevails have been checked against the 1886 text; the account of the surrender, the trials and the pardons is on its p. 8, not p. 7, and it names the second woman shot at the surrender “Mrs. O’Hagg” (see Who died at Kington Fort?). The counts on Who they were now include all 178 people linked to Family Tree.

item.title: 7 Nov 2026: Reading the sources; Two Montana sources; Where Gwendale was; and 6 more
item.description:
• Reading the sources
  • Two Montana sources
  • Where Gwendale was
  • The Deer Lodge paper
  • The groups over time
  • Witnesses at Burton’s trial
  • Fuller’s order for the posse
  • Isabella and James Bowman
  • Newspapers

Reading the sources. The Bibliography now opens with a note on using the secondary literature and a list of common errors in print, from the siege placed at “Manti” to the street burial, with what the records show. A new question on the Questions page asks how the story has been passed down and where those errors come from.

Two Montana sources. Henry Hendrickson’s 1962 interview on the Deer Lodge Valley Morrisites, now online from the University of Montana, is listed under Repositories, and Julie A. Wright’s 2004 thesis “Mormon Movement to Montana” under Bibliography.

Where Gwendale was. Notices in the New North-West place Gwendale, the Montana settlement renamed Morristown in 1878, in the upper Deer Lodge valley near Warm Springs and Lost Creek; by 1883 its school district was called Willow Glen. Gwendale is now marked on the valley map, with roll notes for W. P. Thomas and William W. Thomas. The four Warm Springs homestead claims named in a March 1880 land-office notice (Morgan Evans, Peter Jessen, Daniel James and W. P. Thomas) were all patented in 1880–81 and are now drawn on the map. The paper also settles the link between the names: in March 1882 it reported John R. Eardley’s appointment as postmaster “at Willow Glen on Warm Spring creek, where the Gwendale postoffice formerly was”; his store stood at “Daniel James’ corner.” See Deer Lodge Valley and Newspapers.

The Deer Lodge paper. Seven items from the New North-West of Deer Lodge (1877–86), free on Chronicling America, are now on the Newspapers page. Among them: a Montana post office renamed Morristown in 1878 because many of its people were Morrisites, a description of Davies’s colony in 1877, and the Doves’ visit to preach at the Deer Lodge courthouse in 1885.

The groups over time. A new timeline in the History chronology shows the Morrisite groups side by side on one time scale, from Morris’s church through Soda Springs, Nevada, Cainan’s claim, Omaha, the Montana church, Davies’s Kingdom of Heaven, Parson’s kingdom and the Doves’ Church of the Firstborn, with their leaders and the movements of members between them.

Witnesses at Burton’s trial. Former Morrisites who testified at Burton’s 1879 trial are now noted on the roll: Mary Christoffersen Anderson and Caroline (Karen) Eliason of Soda Springs, Philip Hewitt of Salt Lake City, Emma Thompson Just of the Snake River valley, and, less certainly, Abraham Taylor and Thomas Williams. Mary Anderson, Emma Just and Philip Hewitt now have an 1879 stop on Where they went.

Fuller’s order for the posse. The Documents page now has the Wells–Shaffer correspondence of October 1870, with the text of Acting Governor Frank Fuller’s order of June 11, 1862, requiring Daniel H. Wells to furnish a military posse for the arrest of Joseph Morris.

Isabella and James Bowman. Isabella Bowman, killed at the surrender and the woman Burton was tried for killing in 1879, is now listed among the others named in the sources, with her husband James, who testified at the trial. James was earlier taken to be the John Bowman of the roll; the sources show they were different men. The timeline now gives both of Burton’s indictments: 1870, voided in 1872, and 1877.

Newspapers. A new Newspapers page lists the press coverage by event, from the Sacramento dispatch of June 16, 1862, and its reprints as far as England and Australia, through the 1870 dispute over who commanded at Kington Fort, Burton’s arrest in 1877 and the Salt Lake Tribune letters of 1891, to recent retellings. It also has tips for searching the newspapers. A first pass through Utah Digital Newspapers added the Salt Lake Herald’s daily reports of Burton’s 1879 trial, where former Morrisites testified and gave their homes at the time, and a 1907 interview with Presto Burrell of Connor’s command, who helped escort the colony to Soda Springs.

item.title: 6 Nov 2026: Where they went; Zbaraschuk on Davies, and two more court cases; A map of Morristown; and 4 more
item.description:
• Where they went
  • Zbaraschuk on Davies, and two more court cases
  • A map of Morristown
  • Maps of Kington Fort and the Kingdom of Heaven
  • Places in the Deer Lodge Valley
  • Anaconda and Willow Glen
  • The “seventh angel” before Morris

Where they went. A new animated map follows the people on the 1861–62 roll from Kington Fort to Soda Springs, the Carson Valley, the Deer Lodge Valley, Walla Walla and beyond, year by year, as censuses, land patents, testimony and death records place them. Choose a family to follow it, or tap a dot for the person’s sources.

Zbaraschuk on Davies, and two more court cases. Tony Zbaraschuk’s 1989 Walla Walla College paper on William W. Davies is now in the Bibliography. Its notes point to two more suits against the Davieses (1882 and 1883), now listed with the Davies case files on Repositories.

A map of Morristown. The Morristown page now maps the 1863 settlement at Soda Springs: the Lower Town (mostly under Alexander Reservoir), the probable site of Camp Connor, the markers, the Andersons’ graves in Fairview Cemetery, and the land patents of the families who stayed. Hover over the markers on the Places map to preview each place’s site map.

Maps of Kington Fort and the Kingdom of Heaven. The Kington Fort page now maps the fort and the siege of June 1862 as G. Q. Jones’s plan and Anderson place them: the monument, the fort’s outline, the bowery, the west gate, the slough by the south gate and the posse’s bluffs. The Kingdom of Heaven page maps William W. Davies’s eighty acres, placed from the legal description in the 1881 sheriff’s sale, and Swen O. Hagg’s homestead. Each site is marked as located, approximate or not yet located.

Places in the Deer Lodge Valley. The Deer Lodge Valley page now has a map and a list of the Morrisite sites in the valley, each marked as located, approximate or not yet located: the Lord’s House at Racetrack, the land entries of Morrisite families between Racetrack and Deer Lodge, William Price Thomas’s 1863 settlement on Warm Springs Creek, and Willow Glen, where a reminiscence in the Montana Historical Society places the post office of 1881 beside “an old log church” and the home of William James. Corrections are welcome.

Anaconda and Willow Glen. Volunteers at the Marcus Daly Museum and Archives in Anaconda shared the museum’s Willow Glen photographs, including the Rasmus Rasmussen family in 1915, and pages from Patrick F. Morris’s history of Anaconda on the first Morrisite settlers in the upper Deer Lodge Valley and the wagon train of 1871. See History under the 1870s, Repositories and the Bibliography.

The “seventh angel” before Morris. Kirk Watson points out that the title Morris claimed was already in Latter-day Saint use: W. W. Phelps’s 1844 funeral sermon for Joseph Smith alludes to him as the seventh angel of Revelation 16, a connection first made by Christopher Blythe, and Doctrine and Covenants 88:112 names “Michael, the seventh angel, even the archangel.” See History under 1884 and the Glossary.

item.title: 5 Nov 2026: The Walla Walla court files; The man who went for help; A 1982 newspaper story
item.description:
• The Walla Walla court files
  • The man who went for help
  • A 1982 newspaper story

The Walla Walla court files. The Washington State Archives scanned the two lawsuits against William W. Davies for this guide. The 1880 case brought by three former followers ended in a judgment of $3,225 and the sheriff’s sale of the community’s livestock and its eighty acres in 1881. Its depositions add to the record of several people on the 1861–62 roll: Peter C. Klemgard, who lived at Davies’s camp from 1870 to 1872; Swen O. Hagg, who came to Walla Walla with the first five families in 1867; Niels R. Beck, probably the “Neil A. [or R.?] Beck of Montana” who sent money toward the land; and R. J. Livingstone, who left the Carson Valley for Walla Walla in 1877, as the Carson Valley News reported. Witnesses also describe the community’s teaching of reincarnation. Thanks to Lee Pierce of the archives’ Eastern Region Branch. See Repositories, the roll notes and the reincarnation question.

The man who went for help. Lars Christian Geertsen, one of the men the Morrisites held in their log-house jail in 1862, escaped and carried word to Salt Lake City. A Church History Department profile now confirms that he is the same man who settled at Salmon, Idaho, where he ranched at Geertson Creek and built a log house, later listed on the National Register of Historic Places, whose upstairs dance hall served the community into the 1920s. Readers in Salmon pointed the way. See Lars Christian Geertsen.

A 1982 newspaper story. The Montana Standard of June 19, 1982, ran “Deer Lodge Once Thought to Be Site of Second Coming,” with photographs of the Racetrack church; Kris Pozega, a great-great-niece of George Johnson, brought it to light. See the Bibliography.

item.title: 4 Nov 2026: Where did the reincarnation teaching come from?; What became of them; The 1880 census; and 3 more
item.description:
• Where did the reincarnation teaching come from?
  • What became of them
  • The 1880 census
  • The “Walla Walla Jesus” case
  • Land records
  • Three new pages

Where did the reincarnation teaching come from? With help from Kirk Watson, the question now sets out C. LeRoy Anderson’s theory that Morris took the idea from Charles B. Thompson, and the case against it: the idea was already current among Latter-day Saints in the 1850s, and Morris dated it to a revelation of 1859. It also adds Israel A. J. Dennis, who founded a reincarnationist “Church of the First Born” with no known Morrisite tie, and corrects the chronology on James Brighouse, whose ideas have not been traced to the Morrisites. See Questions and History.

What became of them. The later paths of the people on the roll now have their own section on Who they were, beside the paths that brought them into the movement.

The 1880 census. One census page at Walla Walla shows William W. Davies’s Kingdom of Heaven in the summer it began to break up: Davies, a widower, with Sven Hagg in his house and David Park, Ole Hagg, the Sorensons and others around him, months after the deaths of his sons Arthur and David. The same census finds Erik Eliasson farming in the Deer Lodge Valley while his family stayed at Soda Springs, and settles who John Garrett’s wife was. See William W. Davies and Erik Eliasson.

The “Walla Walla Jesus” case. The 1880 lawsuit against Davies, reported missing from the county courthouse, survives in the Washington State Archives as a territorial court case file, and Whitman College holds copies of depositions and an 1882 photograph of the Davies family and home. See Repositories.

Land records. Federal land patents traced for about twenty roll members and their families, from David Park’s claim in the Carson Valley in 1864 to Walla Walla in 1890, with the Deer Lodge Valley, Soda Springs and Blackfoot between. See the notes on the roll and Repositories.

Three new pages. Niels R. Beck, John Garrett and David Park bring the pages on people of the roll to thirty-seven.

item.title: 3 Nov 2026: The Eliasons and the Christoffersens; The prisoners and the trials; Paths into the movement; and 1 more

  • The prisoners and the trials
  • Paths into the movement

The Eliasons and the Christoffersens. A family group sheet and a 1989 Powell County history add Erik Eliasson’s brother Elias, the family’s move to the Deer Lodge Valley, and the Christoffersens’ road north to Montana. See Erik Eliasson.

The prisoners and the trials. The Deseret News named the ninety-eight men brought before Judge Kinney after the siege in June 1862, and the seven convicted of murder in March 1863, with their sentences. The posse lost two men, not one. See Documents and Questions.

Paths into the movement. Who they were now asks what brought Latter-day Saints to Morris: those who reached Utah in 1859–60 joined at about twice the rate of earlier emigrants. The roll now has 150 names linked to FamilySearch, 30 family groups, and notes on 92 people.

Pages on people of the roll. Thirty-four members now have pages of their own, with what the sources say about them and full citations; look for the page tag on the roll.

Documents and the posse order. A new page gathers the primary documents that can be read online, including Acting Governor Fuller’s order of June 11, 1862, calling out the militia. See Documents.

Who they were. The people on the roll counted by sex, language, age, birthplace, arrival in Utah and where they died, with 91 of them read in the 1860 census. See Who they were.

The Racetrack church in photographs. Twenty photographs taken September 5, 1989, courtesy of Barbara B. Walden, Community of Christ Historic Sites Foundation, open a dated record of the church to 2018, with views of South Weber and the cannonballs. See Images.

The roll of membership. The 1861–62 roll, printed in 1886: 430 names, checked against the pamphlet and searchable. See the Roll of membership.
